h1: Why celestial navigation only closes on a globe
lead: A sextant sight measures one thing: the altitude of a body — its angle above the sea horizon. Everything else in navigation is built on how that altitude changes as you move over the surface. That rate is the whole game, and only one shape of Earth produces the rate ships actually measure.
formula-gloss: a = change in a body's altitude · d = distance moved over the ground toward or away from its sub-point · k = the rate linking them. The last two forms can both be true only if k = 1/R — the signature of a sphere of radius R.
notes-gp: Point a body straight up and you are standing on its geographic position (GP) — the spot where it sits at the zenith. Because the stars are so far away, their light arrives parallel across the whole Earth, so a body's zenith distance (90° − altitude) equals your angular distance from its GP. On a sphere the arc you walk and the angle you turn are locked together by arc = R × angle — that is d = a × R — so k = 1/R is identical everywhere, in every direction, for every body.
callout-constant: The measured constant. Navigators find that 1 arcminute of altitude change = 1 nautical mile of travel toward the GP — which is how the nautical mile was defined. Feed that into d = a/k: with k = 1′/nm, R = 1/k ≈ 3438 nm ≈ 6371 km. The radius drops out of star sights alone, and it matches the Earth's independently-known size.
h2-3d: See it in 3D: four sights, one fix
lead-3d: Each star stands above its ground position (GP); the observer measures its altitude and computes a distance d = a/k, which draws a circle of position on the surface around that GP. The flat model gets every advantage: its star height H is calibrated so that sight ① works perfectly. The other three sights follow. Drag either canvas to orbit the shared camera.
globe-cap: Globe. With k = 1/R, all four circles d = a/k pass through the observer — one point satisfies every sight simultaneously. This is a celestial fix, performed at sea every day.
flat-cap: Flat plane. Stars at height H over the same GPs. Even with H tuned so circle ① hits the observer exactly, circles ②–④ fall short (red gaps) — because atan(r/H) isn't proportional to r. No single H fixes all four.
fix-table-caption: The four sights: measured altitude → d = a/k, versus what the flat model's circles actually do
refr-note: Refraction shown — solid line: the apparent (refracted) direction the sextant actually points at; dashed line: the star's true geometric direction. Air bends light downward, lifting each apparent altitude by ≈1′/tan h (Bennett). The bend is drawn ×{exag} exaggerated to be visible — real corrections are arcminutes: {vals}.
h2-rate: Test it yourself: is k constant?
lead-rate: A body sits directly over its sub-point. The globe drops its altitude at a fixed rate; the flat-plane model (body at height H) does not. Watch the two rate columns.
rate-table-caption: Altitude of a body above its sub-point, with the local rate of altitude change (arcminutes per nautical mile)
rate-note: The globe rate holds flat at {k} ′/nm — that is k = 1/R, giving R = 1/k ≈ {Rnm} nm ≈ {Rkm} km. The flat-model rate slides from steep near the sub-point to shallow far away, so there is no single k.
lead-exp2: Measure the altitude of Polaris. Drive a known distance due north along a straight road. Measure it again. The star has climbed — the question is by how much.
exp2-out: IV d = {d} km north, starting at {lat}°N. Flat prediction: Polaris rises {flat}°. Globe prediction: Polaris rises {globe}°. They differ by {diff}° ({diffArcmin}′).
exp2-verdict: Verdict rule: the globe says the rise is always {globe}° for {d} km — the same everywhere. The flat model cannot hold that: from 15°N it predicts {at15}°, from 60°N {at60}°.
callout-why-fails: Why the plane fails, in one line. On a flat plane a body at finite height can never reach the horizon (atan(H/x) stays positive), so the Sun would never set; different bodies would need different heights H and return contradictory fixes; and k would change with where you stand. The globe uses a single radius R and one k = 1/R for the Sun, the Moon and every star at once.
